name: Apache JMeter
summary: The long-standing open-source load tester: a Java app where you build test plans in a GUI, then run them headless with many threads as virtual users.
intro: A JMeter test plan is a tree of elements saved as an XML `.jmx` file. A thread group says how many virtual users to start, how fast to ramp them up and how often to loop; each user is a Java thread that runs the whole plan on its own. Samplers send the requests: HTTP and HTTPS, SOAP and REST, JDBC queries, JMS, LDAP, FTP, mail, TCP and shell commands. Extractors pull values such as session tokens out of HTML, JSON or XML responses, timers add think time, and assertions mark responses as failed. JMeter works at the protocol level: it is not a browser and does not run the JavaScript in a page.

You build and debug a plan in the desktop GUI, often by recording a browser session through its proxy, and then run it in CLI mode, which writes every sample to a results file and can generate an HTML dashboard of response times, throughput and errors. The docs warn never to run real load from the GUI. For more load than one machine can make, a controller sends the plan over Java RMI to `jmeter-server` processes on other machines, which all run the same plan. A Backend Listener can stream live results to InfluxDB or Graphite for Grafana. JMeter is free under Apache 2.0. The latest release is 5.6.3 from January 2024, which needs Java 8 or later; the main branch is preparing 6.0, which will need Java 17.
strengths: Most plans need no code: record a session, add extractors and assertions in the GUI, and save
Covers more than HTTP: JDBC, JMS, LDAP, FTP, mail, TCP and plain Java requests from the same tool
Built-in distributed mode and a ready HTML report, with no paid service needed
A built-in Backend Listener streams live results to InfluxDB or Graphite, so you can watch a test in Grafana while it runs
limits: One thread per virtual user, with a 1 GB heap by default: the docs estimate 1,000 to 2,000 threads per machine, so large tests need distributed mode or more memory
`.jmx` files are verbose XML written by the GUI, awkward to review in pull requests compared with k6, Gatling or Locust tests written as code
Distributed mode uses RMI, which expects the machines on one subnet with the same JMeter and Java versions and firewall ports opened
Slow releases: nothing since 5.6.3 in January 2024, though the code is still worked on for 6.0

snippet.title: Run a saved plan headless, then across several load machines
source: # Build and debug checkout.jmx in the GUI first (just run `jmeter`), then:
#  -n  CLI mode (no GUI)        -t  the test plan
#  -l  raw sample results       -e -o  HTML dashboard into an empty folder
# More heap than the default 1 GB for big thread counts
# Distributed: start `jmeter-server` on each load machine, then
# each remote server runs the same plan; results come back to this machine

story: Stefano Mazzocchi, at the Apache Software Foundation, wrote the first version of JMeter to measure the performance of Apache JServ, the Java servlet engine that Apache Tomcat later replaced. Its changelog starts with version 1.0.1 in January 1999; by July of that year 1.4 had added cookies, HTTP authentication and new result visualizers.

The project later redesigned the GUI and added functional-testing features, then grew samplers for databases, messaging and directories. It became a top-level Apache project in November 2011, with its own project management committee. 5.6.3 came out in January 2024; since then the main branch has been preparing 6.0, which needs Java 17, stops sending expired cookies and drops the MongoDB sampler.

choices.choice: Pure Java, with a desktop GUI
choices.why: It ran anywhere Java did, and testers could build plans by pointing and clicking instead of writing code.

choices.choice: Work at the protocol level, not in a browser
choices.why: It was written to measure a server, Apache JServ, so it sends the requests itself; it never renders pages or runs their JavaScript, which means it measures the server, not what a browser does.

Each thread runs the plan from top to bottom, independently, with its own variables, so a plan reads like one user’s session; the price is memory per user, and the project lists a thread-pool or async core as a future goal.
